item.title: On the AHM’s awkward position on the Riemann Hypothesis being solved
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: A response to AHM's reaction to the claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a couple of posts ago.
item.content:encoded:
Dan Romik, Professor at UC Davis and founder of Rhombic Research

In reply to AHM Statement on the Announced Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis by AHM communications group

Written without AI using ReelDocs

This is a post about the Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) and a statement they made this Friday (November 20, 2026).

Who are they

The AHM are a group of people who describe themselves in these words:

The Association for Human Mathematics protects mathematics as a human endeavor against the threat of artificial intelligence. We work to maintain the independence of the mathematical community from the encroachment of corporate interest. In light of the grave societal, environmental, and economic impacts of the AI industry and the threat of unfettered AI growth, we strive not to be complicit.

What they said on November 20, 2026

Following Levent Alpöge’s announcement of his proof of GRH, the AHM issued a statement titled “AHM Statement on the Announced Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis“. Click the link to read it in full. Below I quote the statement with my own commentary explaining why essentially none of what they are saying makes any sense.

Today, November 20, 2026, a mathematician at Anthropic announced the existence of an AI-generated Lean program confirming the Riemann Hypothesis, long a guiding open problem in mathematics.

Yep.

This announcement is a major departure from traditional methods in mathematical research, representing a new value system put forward by AI corporations that foregrounds technical validity of logical statements over accountability, clarity, accessibility, and understanding.

I can agree with “This announcement is a major departure from traditional methods in mathematical research”. But the part about this “representing a new value system” is a serious bit of editorializing. What does it mean to “foreground” technical validity over other things? In what sense is it the “AI corporations” who are “putting forward” this new value system? And in any case, why does AHM get to decide what should be “foregrounded” and what not? As it happens, I and many other mathematicians consider “technical validity” (which is usually referred to as “validity” without the belittling modifier “technical”) to be one of the most important qualities of any new mathematical work. When we referee a paper, one of the most important questions we are asked to weigh on is whether the paper is correct. The other crucial element of whether a paper is good is whether it proves something interesting and important. By those criteria, a correct proof of the Riemann hypothesis would certainly check the main boxes in terms of whether it should be published. Is this really a new value system that prizes validity? No; it’s been forever the case that mathematicians considered validity to be one of the most important things to care about, and probably the number one thing.

As for the part about “clarity, accessibility, and understanding”: I totally agree that clarity, accessibility and understanding are important. I want those things too; everyone does, even, I’m sure, Levent Alpöge himself. We all want those things for RH, and we will pursue them with vigor. But Rome wasn’t built in a day. If an AI model allows us to make the first step and obtain a correct, “technically valid” proof of RH, why is that a bad thing? Surely this counts as progress towards the ultimate lofty goals of “understanding” etc., doesn’t it? And if you absolutely insist that a 1-gigabyte Lean proof is just a distraction and adds literally nothing useful, well, you are free to just ignore it, aren’t you? Just carry on with your pursuit of human understanding and the other things. Why waste your time writing statements?

And as for the part about “accountability”: I am confused. What could the notion of “accountability” possibly mean for a claimed proof of a theorem? My brain tries and fails to assign a meaning to such a thing. I’ve published many papers in my life and never imagined anyone would say that I am “accountable” for those papers. Honestly, I wish my math research had the kind of impact on the world that would justify using a word like “accountability” in connection with it. Sadly, this has not been the case: no one is asking for me to be accountable for my moving sofas.

At this time, no human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document.

Maybe this is true, but there are all kinds of questionable premises this sentence seems to assume. Why is it a desirable thing for a document with a proof of an important conjecture to have a human who is responsible for it (whatever that even means)? Why is the lack of a human who understands the proof a disqualifying factor?

Neither can any mathematician confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.

This is both factually false (or so misleading as to be essentially false) and again assumes a premise that is itself false. The false part is that no one can confirm with certainty that the proof is correct. In fact the Lean community and Lean FRO have stated confidently that “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct”. You can quibble that they can’t actually “confirm with certainty”; that’s still essentially false, and leaves you as your only remaining rhetorical escape hatch to take such an absolutist position on the meaning of “confirm with certainty” that any reasonable person would involuntarily roll their eyes at you.

Second, the aspect of this sentence that involves assuming a false premise is the implicit assumption that human-authored papers don’t suffer from the exact same (or worse) flaw of lack of “full certainty”. They absolutely do. When Andrew Wiles announced his proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 1993, could he “confirm with full certainty” that his proof is correct? No, he couldn’t, because as it turned out, his proof actually had a serious gap that took more than a year to correct. Did people imply that he was doing something wrong or evil by publishing his initial proof? No, nobody did. Where were you then, AHM? Where were you on numerous other occasions where mathematicians put their credibility on the line by releasing raw, unpolished, very long proofs of major theorems that they couldn’t possibly “confirm with full certainty” were correct, and indeed occasionally turned out to be not exactly correct?

Worse, this corporate model of proof production seems designed to excuse humans from responsibility for scientific work.

“[S]eems designed to” is weasel phrasing. It doesn’t seem designed to do those things to me, but in any case this isn’t really saying anything worth arguing with.

Instead, this model asks scientists to entrust their research to machines that AI corporations control.

One can reasonably be concerned about the state of the world and various specific implications of developments in AI, including the fact that AI corporations’ control of AI technology, which is becoming critical to doing lots of things (particularly math research), may put scientists in the position of needing to entrust some of their research to these corporations. Okay, I concede that this is a valid point. But what does it have to do with the proof the Riemann hypothesis? If AI corporations actually did something good on one Friday in November 2026, isn’t the intellectually honest position to at least acknowledge they did it even if you think everything else they do is bad? And conversely, isn’t there something dishonest about using even that event, which most reasonable people see as a remarkable achievement to celebrate, as an opportunity for yet more soapboxing about how evil and problematic AI is?

Autonomous computer programs that investigate deep mathematical questions are now instruments of power in scientific research, and scientific power enables other types of power that can directly threaten human lives. This power is now concentrated in the hands of AI companies that seem increasingly untethered from the interests of human society. We believe that AI corporations urgently require democratic oversight. Milestones such as the Riemann Hypothesis are used by AI companies as little more than publicity for the superintelligence that they wish to build. We are gravely concerned that this uncontrolled growth poses a threat to society writ large.

Look, AHM: why don’t you just come out and say “We hate AI and think it’s evil”? It’s shorter and clearer and contains the exact same information that your convoluted paragraph delivers.

Mathematicians have seen their world inverted by AI disruption in the last several months, and we have experienced firsthand how AI impacts human communities in practice. AI corporations hold an impoverished view of intelligence and human achievement. As a model for scientific research, the overproduction of unreadable mathematical documents pales in comparison to the richness of the mathematical dialogue that humans have conducted for millennia. What makes the Riemann Hypothesis valuable is its role in guiding the development of large areas of modern mathematics. Today’s announcement builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way. Rather than accepting this model, we urge mathematicians to build a future where our research is free from dependence on AI models and their corporate owners.

Hmmph. For a group of people who complain about unreadable documents, you people sure have trouble making your own documents readable enough to send a clear message. You come across as bitter and frustrated curmudgeons. You complain that “Today’s announcement … fails to advance mathematical understanding”, implying that only you get to decide what mathematical understanding is and what counts as advancing it, and that the only standard by which new work is measured is whether it immediately, on the very same day it is released, improves mathematical understanding according to your definitions. These positions come across as weird and unreasonable and quite off-putting.

At the end of the day, the impression I’m getting is that, as Jared Lichtman amusingly suggested, the AHM members basically support “AHMish mathematics”.

(With apologies to the Amish who I’m sure are all super nice and decent and reasonable people. )

Crossposted from my blog (slightly revised).

Received 24 November 2026.

item.title: I want MSE, not MO.
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “For far too many people—myself included—it has become an identity. That is a terrible thing. If we place such importance on the emotional dimensions of mathematics, then it should not be pursued as a profession. What direction should the future mathematics community take? […]”
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Undergraduate student

For far too many people—myself included—it has become an identity. That is a terrible thing. If we place such importance on the emotional dimensions of mathematics, then it should not be pursued as a profession.

What direction should the future mathematics community take? Since we all value community consensus, let’s look at the two largest communities: Math StackExchange and MathOverflow. Compare MSE and MO: MO is more rigorous, higher-level, and precise (Like current AI)—but MSE is far more human and engaging. I choose MSE, not MO.

We should be able to complete homework, ask interesting questions, and make friends—not everything needs to be turned into a research question. While both types of communities have value, the number of active participants—influenced, of course, by barriers to entry—reveals what people actually want.

Received 30 October 2026.

item.title: Describing Structures and Beyond: Why Writing Mathematics Still Matters in the Age of AI
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: I believe that mathematics is not pure logic suspended in a vacuum, but rather a product of history and culture. Treating math merely as a technical tool that can be deconstructed causes us to lose the precious humanistic essence embedded within it.
item.content:encoded:
Christoph Mark, independent researcher, unaffiliated

AI disclosure

(Disclaimer: I’ve used AI to bounce ideas and receive feedback to what I’ve written. I’ve however renounced the need to polish my English with the help of AI, since I think my original wording is important to preserve the meaning of the text.)

I’ve often pondered the question of what message a mathematical piece of writing can convey beyond the formal information about hard abstraction1: definitions, theorems, proofs, lemmas, propositions, more proofs and maybe a short historical overview of what others have done before. By a message (“Botschaft”) conveyed, I mean any sort of worldview, convictions, beliefs or experience of the author. At a first glance, it might be hopeless to convey a message beyond the facts through mathematics, but this essay is designed to convince you of the opposite to some degree and maybe that such a message may be even important and the prevalent driving force to write mathematics in the first place in the age of AI, predominantly, but ever since for some authors.

Concerning the messages which are suitable to be expressed, I focus on unpersonal, deindividualized, unbiographical messages, as I came to the conclusion that only those can be communicated clearly through our language and in a way comprehensible for others. If we start to speak on a microscopic level about every subjective feeling, I’m under the impression that the reader often can’t relate to what is meant, which is mostly due to our inability to communicate clearly a subjective state of mind; thus, a certain level of abstraction is the presupposition of any organized text.

Yet, I’ve spoken about sharing an experience through mathematics in the first paragraph which I want to specify: I’m often under the impression a common people or a common time or any common group shares an experience it is paradoxically unable to share at once and only through science or what is considered mostly the humanities but not only. This unshared-shared experience emerges often with a certain distance in time in the historical analysis when we can speak in hindsight about the “Zeitgeist” of a certain period or, for example, in art history about a certain movement which was typical for that time. In this sense, a movement might be typical in its universal deindividualized messages and still individual. The sense of individuality I think about is, for example, seen in individuals like Nietzsche, who, with his radical critique of Christianity, was an almost unknown outsider in his lifetime, yet is declared a typical German of his time and even timeless by the afterworld. I sometimes think this phenomenon of excluding an individual in his individuality just to celebrate him later, maybe after his death, is in itself typical German.

One might ask now how to “transport“2 a message through mathematics and everybody will think through style and exposition. But I personally do not think of style and exposition and the technical abilities of the author as a purpose of its own sake, I rather think of the best mathematics of those writings, which most accurately and nuanced put forward the message by any means. And, indeed, it’s this type of mathematics I’ve always appreciated the most reading independently from its prevalent content. It’s this mathematics I’ve endeavored to write as much as I can and as much as my intellectual means permit. It’s this mathematics where while reading you get a grasp of its time and its context, where you get to know the author, I think, is most valuable. In this regard, mathematics has to live also as a historical science because some texts never get old or outdated and are worthwhile reading even today and again. I don’t think we should deprive students from reading primary sources just because “a proof and an argument is stable and can be presented by everyone”3 and I’ve never done so as a student.

Another way to transport a message in mathematics is by choice of the subject and the methods. Philosophical discussions in mathematics, orally and most notably in writing, are often considered cancerous and discarded. On the rare occasions a math professor at the Technical University of Munich, an institution I disagree with the way mathematics is taught in a positivistic way, dropped a philosophical comment during a lecture, he said that there will never be schools in mathematics because of a strict notion of truth. Every informed mathematician can refute this claim by observing there is and was, for example, a French school of mathematics, a Japanese, a German or whatever. Thus, by choosing in our work a specific subject matter and a specific method, we can align ourselves within a tradition and school and therefore itself make a statement together with the philosophical implications of the messages of this school or tradition.

I want to end this essay with a few examples which underpin the ideas developed by naming some “good” pieces of mathematical writings and authors in the sense above. Everybody will think first rightfully of Bourbaki and closely related Grothendieck’s school of mathematics. Indeed, it’s one example where mathematics evolved around the Zeitgeist after the Second World War (“Stunde Null”) and reflects French structuralism in a perfect way. We see similar abstract endeavors all around in France of this time, for example, in Le Corbusier’s architecture or the Paris art world fight between figuration and abstraction, and of Paris as opposition to New York as the new art metropolis. We see this wrestle of the time also in the German movement of “Informel”, which even picked up nuances from science in its art, like Einstein’s general relativity or what they called the fourth dimension and shaped space, although admittedly late (cf. Norbert Kricke). But this adventure of the “Nachkriegszeit” is not an isolated phenomenon and we can consider other authors as well. To my mind comes second Euler with his personal strong Christian beliefs and that of his time, which were lived throughout his life and deeds, his thirteen children, his endless pursuit of mathematics through his whole life and despite blindness and fate, and are equally well reflected in his playful, witty math style which makes the process visible and is open to everyone: It is told he even used his analysis book to teach his servants mathematics. On the contrary at around the same time, we have Gauß with his almost aristocratic style of the sublime in the sense of Kant which mostly reflects his motto “Pauca sed matura!”.

I could elaborate on these and other examples with anecdotes but I don’t want to overcharge this essay and it’s not its primary purpose. For me, it’s important that the philosophical line of thought about worthwhile mathematics is even reflected in the philosophical structure of this essay. I want to end with a final thought about mathematics and AI which is currently in vogue and also the topic of this blog. I hope the essay makes in some sense clear: If mathematics is done “right”, in the way I like to do it and appreciate it ever since, there’s no reason to fear any AI-assisted mathematics at all, but rather there’s a total net benefit in it that it opens up and democratises mathematics and knowledge for a more general public.

Received 6 October 2026.

  1. The notion of “hard abstraction” actually comes from the reception history of the œuvre of Gerhard Richter – an artist who I admire less than the art historians who have written about him – but as we speak often in analogies about mathematics, it fits here as well to describe a piece of writing with a primary focus on hard facts. ︎
  2. In this context, Proust has coined the term “transport” for what he wanted to transport of his personality or any author’s personality through a piece of literature. He had the opinion that an exceptional personality is key for any exceptional writing. While this might be true in some contexts and even mathematics, we rather focus on the notion of deindividualized messages, which can be even individual in the sense explained above. ︎
  3. This is indeed, in my opinion, a false idea of Yuri Manin. In an interview on a tour of mockery, he asked: “Who reads Newton?” ︎

item.title: A call for greater collaboration
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “Recently I've learned that two separate groups of people have been using AI to make rapid progress on a couple of projects that I had been working on, as well as one problem which is a PhD student's ongoing thesis project. To be clear, I use AI in research also, and I am not upset that they are exploring what they are interested in. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Kimball Martin, Professor at Osaka Metropolitan University

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

Recently I’ve learned that two separate groups of people have been using AI to make rapid progress on a couple of projects that I had been working on, as well as one problem which is a PhD student’s ongoing thesis project. To be clear, I use AI in research also, and I am not upset that they are exploring what they are interested in. What would bother me is to discover at a late stage that we have both been doing the same things “in private”. And if the student’s thesis came to be considered unacceptable, that would be a disaster.

Much has been said about the idea that we should value exposition over priority of discovery. Maybe. But we are not there yet. And losing the thrill of being the first to discover something, and then sharing it with others, would remove much of the joy of research. Instead, I want to propose something else.

Let’s try being more collaborative within our community. Many people may feel an urge to be more secretive now. I’m not saying to advertise everything you’re doing publicly. But if we have more large working groups within the community, then there is less of a need to rush things out because of real or imagined competition—partly because many of your potential competitors are now collaborators and because you may have more projects going on at one time. There will be less duplication of effort, and collaboration may make our end results better or more impactful.

What would it mean if large collaborations were common? Students may not have to produce solo papers for their PhD theses, but contributing to group collaborations would be sufficient. (This is already the case in many fields.) How would people be evaluated for jobs and grants? Maybe with some combination of publication record and recommendations like today. Maybe there will be an imperfect yet not horrible system of assigning credit for large collaborations. But if we all work with each other more, and know each other more, it should be easier to make evaluations that are less dependent on comparing one person’s publication record with another’s.

I am not saying we should all collaborate in large groups. But however things are in your community now, it will be hard to stay abreast of what others are doing without more effort towards communication and coordination. In fact, I am using the term collaboration rather loosely. I also mean the coordination efforts that many people already do—e.g., multiple small groups/individuals communicating and planning with each other, but writing papers separately.

In the case of one of the problems I mentioned above, I first learned about the situation from a collaborator, who heard about it from one of their collaborators. (In the other case, someone who was working on the problem just emailed me directly). After initially thinking that we may just have to abandon the project, I decided to email the other group to let them know what we had been doing and suggest we coordinate. Then we met on Zoom, and shared what we were doing with each other. It turned out that neither of our works subsumed the other. In our case we decided to continue focusing on the non-overlapping parts separately, and keep each other updated, with the idea that we may join forces at the next stage.

Practically, what do I have in mind, you may wonder. I don’t have in mind public open projects like the Polymath Project or Terry Tao’s recent Siegel zeroes challenge, or massive 200-person collaborations, though those could be part of it. I imagine collaborations that are larger than the typical 2-4 person collaborations—perhaps 5-10, 10-20 or 20-50 person collaborations. Some workshops foster collaborations at these scales, but normally only for a short time, and often these are low-priority side projects for participants. But if you’ve been part of such a project, you may have an idea of what I mean. They involve real human interaction, just like typical small collaborations, but the organization and dynamics may be different.

Large collaborations rarely sprout up organically; real effort and organization are required to start these. Here are some naive thoughts on how to begin:

  • Frequent communication between different researchers/groups is key; talk to others as much as you are able—activities like going to conferences, nearby seminars, and seminar meals, or inviting visitors, present lots of opportunities for more communication
  • If you are exploring a problem with AI and making rapid progress, don’t race to get out a paper on your own (see also slow maths); contact others who are likely to be interested and see if they want to discuss it and possibly join you
  • Organize a workshop or special program that encourages large group discussions and collaborations; from a funding perspective, some could be in-person, some virtual and some hybrid
  • It is easier to organize something after forming a core group of people with a shared goal; try to find a few people you trust with common interests and begin from there
  • Zulip spaces can be used to help coordinate/organize interest in projects or workshops (e.g., the Proofs and Prompts Zulip space; I also have a dormant Zulip for such purposes in number theory/automorphic forms which could be revived if there is interest)
  • I personally favor real collaborations with regular meetings and communication; for larger collaborations, one can break the group into smaller teams for specific tasks; meetings within teams and meetings among team representatives may be more frequent than meetings as one large group; this involves more hierarchy/organization than academic mathematicians are used to in research
  • Different collaborations have different dynamics; there’s no one-size-fits-all best practice
  • Lots of ideas and attempts at even 2-person collaborations don’t pan out, at least not right away; don’t get discouraged if it takes time to find the right group or project
  • If you have other suggestions, please leave them in the comments!

Further thoughts on managing large collaborations

While I am far from an expert in large collaborations, I was encouraged to expand on this aspect. In mathematics, it’s a common view that the time needed to finish a project is inversely proportional to the number of authors. My experience corroborates this, but it also doesn’t have to be this way. First, I think we can look to other fields and industry for best practices for how to manage large projects. Two essays about this from other fields, which I think apply to mathematics with minor changes, are Ten Simple Rules for a Successful Collaboration and Ten simple rules for collaboratively writing a multi-authored paper.

What I have to add to the above 2 pieces is mostly about planning and managing expectations:

  • Collaborating with people requires compromise. Understand going in that people won’t go about things the way you think they should (and sometimes that will be worse, but sometimes better).
  • Know that both work with AI and large collaborations are new for most of us, and we are all figuring out how to do things; be understanding and forgiving about your missteps and others’. So experiment with strategies and see what people like and don’t like.
  • 1-3 people should be in charge of organization and leading the project. These roles require interpersonal and organizational skills; don’t just pick people with the most seniority or mathematical ideas.
  • As much as possible, try to set clear expectations and (hoped-for) timelines. For instance, there could be a period of open discussion for 1-2 weeks to come up with goals and plans of attack. Then, either by a democratic or top-down process, decide on a plan, see who wants to work on this plan, and on what aspects. Set working groups with planned inter- and intra-group meetings, and naive goals for when to finish what tasks. Possibly repeat this process at key stages.
  • Try to keep goals more concrete and tangible than open-ended. Break-up into manageable subgoals, and require regular meetings/progress reports to keep everyone on track. E.g., in Stage 1, Group A will prove Theorem 1; Group B will prove Theorem 2; Group C will prove and implement Algorithm X. Each group aims to write up their work separately within 3 months. All groups will come together for monthly meetings for status updates and help requests. Then plan Stage 2 together, where everyone combines these results to get Big Theorem.
  • Try to set/come to a consensus on expectations as much as possible in advance, with the understanding that you may renegotiate expectations later. In particular, agree on how you will and will not use AI.
  • Trust is paramount. Build trust by being transparent about the decision process, and what different groups are doing, and by listening to other people’s opinions.
  • Don’t work on another individual or group’s tasks, especially using AI, without asking them first.
  • Make contingency plans for when it inevitably happens that, for whatever reason (health, other responsibilities, …), someone cannot contribute or complete their tasks on a satisfactory timeline. For example, there could be an advance agreement that the project will go on without indefinitely waiting on people, and they will stay as co-authors and contribute what they can unless they opt out of the project.
  • Relatedly, upon review stages of the work, set time limits for feedback and comments.
  • Understand that everyone will not contribute “equally”, and that this is fine. If desired, a contributions statement could be added. Be generous about acknowledging others’ contributions and communicate openly to make sure you are all on the same page.

Thanks to John Voight, Sachi Hashimoto, Roi Docampo, and Proofs and Prompts hosts for some feedback on drafts of this post. AI tools were used for light proofreading and searching for relevant links.

Received 6 November 2026, revised 21 November 2026.

item.title: A mathematical community?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “This is an answer to Isabelle Gallagher, President of SMF (Société Mathématique de France). Her proposals are based on two assumptions which are worth a debate. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Jean-Michel Kantor, Emeritus from IMJ (Institut Mathématique de Jussieu), mathematician and historian of mathematics

In reply to Slow Maths by Isabelle Gallagher

This is an answer to Isabelle Gallagher, President of SMF (Société Mathématique de France).

Her proposals are based on two assumptions which are worth a debate:

1. The notion of “mathematical community”

Recent events and publishing materials coming from various countries and continents, in particular from USA and Europe, show that a world mathematical community does not exist and that – if it ever existed – is in the process of disruption.

For example the proposals of Sergiu Klainerman1 and the practice of American mathematicians, involving gigantic amounts of dollars invested in AI-laboratories, reflect the local practices of a supposed “American mathematical community” without mentioning any community outside of Silicon Valley and/or Princeton.

2. Science and technique

Mathematics is confronted not to a scientific debate involving the mathematical practice but to an imposed debate involving a technology, submitted to different laws, in particular, as was expressed by Dennis Gabor (1900–1979, physicist, Nobel Prize in 1971 for the invention of holography) with Gabor’s law:

“What can be done technically will necessarily be done, sooner or later.”2

Applied to AI, juiced up with billions of dollars of the economico-political US domination (till when?) – a dimension surprisingly never mentioned in comments from our American mathematician colleagues.

  1. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29713 ︎
  2. « Ce qui peut être fait techniquement sera fait nécessairement ». Also stated by Jacques Ellul in France. ︎

Received 6 November 2026.

item.title: Homage to Gold Miners
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “The age of steel began with little cause for dread. We worked the stubborn earth and earned our daily bread. We forged a metal wand whose word was loud and clear. The gold we had was real, no pyrite hiding here. And when we struck a vein, it put an end to doubt. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Kei Beauduin, Master’s student at Kyushu University

AI disclosure

The author conceived the ideas, used an LLM to draft the poem,1 and refined it with the model.

The age of steel began with little cause for dread.
We worked the stubborn earth and earned our daily bread.

We forged a metal wand whose word was loud and clear.
The gold we had was real, no pyrite hiding here.

And when we struck a vein, it put an end to doubt.
We learned to lean on it. Its verdict bore us out.

Then came a company with engines built to bore.
They barely scratched the dirt; a spoon could dig up more.

But year by year they grew with jaws of tempered steel.
They split the mountain’s spine and made the granite kneel.

Our wand still vouched for gold amid the shattered stone.
They heaped the dirty spoil in mountains of their own.

One day their trucks arrived and backed into our yard.
They tipped their cargo out without the least regard.

It stank beneath the sun, with treasure buried deep,
Enough to claim our days and rob us of our sleep.

No doubt we’d reach the gold, but there was still a cost.
We’d pay in time and sweat, with some dignity lost.

We took our shovels up. What else were we to do?
Then bent our backs to dig straight through the reeking poo.

Received 9 October 2026.

  1. Inspired by David Fisher’s remark about writing a haiku. ︎

item.title: On Premature Discovery
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Suppose we fault an AI solution to a motivating problem for preempting the development of mathematical theory. Human solutions deserve no exemption on that ground.
item.content:encoded:
Florian Lengyel, independent researcher, retired from the City University of New York

AI disclosure

AI-use disclosure: ChatGPT assisted with drafting, revision, and source checking.

Human-use disclosure: The author revised AI-generated dilution of original text until AI relented.

Suppose we fault an AI solution to a motivating problem for preempting the development of mathematical theory. Human solutions deserve no exemption on that ground.

Science and technology have repeatedly unsettled humanity’s pretensions to exceptional status. Copernicus displaced Earth from the center of the cosmos; Darwin placed humanity within the evolutionary history of the animal kingdom. Machines have since defeated world champions at chess and Go. OpenAI now reports a proof of Sogge’s local smoothing conjecture in every dimension, a refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and an existence proof for four-dimensional pure Yang–Mills theory, with Lean formalizations of these results.

Lander and Parkin refuted Euler’s conjecture on sums of like powers by direct computer search in 1966. On the same principle, they should have left it standing for the theories it might yet inspire.

Humanity cannot plead exceptional status to escape the charge of premature discovery: depriving mathematics of the theories it might have developed had its practitioners been less successful. If this is the offense, distinction in mathematics measures the offender’s depravity.

Therefore, ipso facto, the great problem-solvers must be condemned.

Received 28 October 2026, revised 3 November 2026.

item.title: AHM Statement on the Announced Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Statement of the Association for Human Mathematics
item.content:encoded:
AHM communications group

Today, November 20, 2026, a mathematician at Anthropic announced the existence of an AI-generated Lean program confirming the Riemann Hypothesis, long a guiding open problem in mathematics.

This announcement is a major departure from traditional methods in mathematical research, representing a new value system put forward by AI corporations that foregrounds technical validity of logical statements over accountability, clarity, accessibility, and understanding. At this time, no human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document. Neither can any mathematician confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct. Worse, this corporate model of proof production seems designed to excuse humans from responsibility for scientific work. Instead, this model asks scientists to entrust their research to machines that AI corporations control.

Autonomous computer programs that investigate deep mathematical questions are now instruments of power in scientific research, and scientific power enables other types of power that can directly threaten human lives. This power is now concentrated in the hands of AI companies that seem increasingly untethered from the interests of human society. We believe that AI corporations urgently require democratic oversight. Milestones such as the Riemann Hypothesis are used by AI companies as little more than publicity for the superintelligence that they wish to build. We are gravely concerned that this uncontrolled growth poses a threat to society writ large.

Mathematicians have seen their world inverted by AI disruption in the last several months, and we have experienced firsthand how AI impacts human communities in practice. AI corporations hold an impoverished view of intelligence and human achievement. As a model for scientific research, the overproduction of unreadable mathematical documents pales in comparison to the richness of the mathematical dialogue that humans have conducted for millennia. What makes the Riemann Hypothesis valuable is its role in guiding the development of large areas of modern mathematics. Today’s announcement builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way. Rather than accepting this model, we urge mathematicians to build a future where our research is free from dependence on AI models and their corporate owners.

Crossposted from the AHM website.

Received 20 November 2026.

item.title: Artificial mathematics
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: As a current Director of Graduate Studies in a math department, I wanted to write something to encourage our students and potential students, to reassure them of the abiding importance of human mathematics. The result is not practical advice, but maybe an update of Roosevelt’s line about fear for the AI age.
item.content:encoded:
Matt Kerr, Professor and Director of Graduate Studies, Department of Mathematics at Washington University in St. Louis

The unofficial logo of my tech-magnet high school was a computerized version of Hokusai’s massive blue wave, and with the OpenAI slop drop1 it finally feels like that wave is poised to flatten the far more creative ecosystem to which I fled. Encountering Strogatz’s essay2 “A Mathematician Reads the AI Future” in its wake, I had hoped for a more vigorous defense of an intellectual tradition which, with philosophy, has always belonged at the nerve center of Arts & Sciences despite being emphatically neither. While he worries that something deeply human could be lost if, in the rush to ride that wave, we let verification replace understanding and hand the process of its development over to machines, the essay ends with a sense of communal resignation.

My initial thought, from the stories Strogatz tells, was that events are driving a subtle but significant wedge between pure and applied mathematics and mathematicians. Applied math is oriented toward well-defined external goals, like improving imaging or data compression algorithms, and has the most obvious and immediate value to society. To its practitioners, AI simply feels like another tool, like a microscope or telescope. While it may change the stage of reasoning at which the computer becomes involved in their work, this is nothing to be “ashamed” of, as I heard a department chair say at a recent AMS discussion of AI.

If that’s true, then perhaps applied mathematicians, and even some pure mathematicians who are oriented toward knowing rather than understanding, don’t share the sense of loss that pure mathematicians are facing right now. Strogatz avers that despite his sympathy with pure math, he believes that math is a science, and that there are external “truths” that exist without humans, and which we discover. (In fact, he gets a pure mathematician to say this.) Hardy also makes the latter error in his otherwise moving “Apology”.3 Aside from the fact that science doesn’t deal with truths, it deals with theories, there are two problems with externalizing math from humans in this way.

The first is that what mathematicians regard as logical reasoning is merely a form of grammar, or a grammar of form, constantly reshaped with definitions and conventions. It helps us to clarify and distill our ideas and frame them in communicable shapes, in much the same way that a poet or composer uses sonnets or sonata form or polytonal counterpoint as a clarifying fire and vessel for their own. There are no fewer possibilities for a work of mathematics than for a verse play or an opera; but just as with monkeys and Shakespeare, it’s humans who need to decide what to write and what is beautiful or important. In my mind, pure math is not about what correctly aligns with something which is “out there”, which I suppose was an acceptable view in the so-called Enlightenment when people didn’t know any better, but what constitutes a strong poem with the potential to move and influence humans.

In short, the representationalist view of mathematics is anti-humanistic, and also (in my view) incorrect. If we hand our subject over to computers, they will generate everything — and thus nothing, as in the “pleroma” of Jung’s Sermons to the Dead — according to whatever state of grammar was programmed into Lean as the Project 2025 of a misguided gang of mathematical technocrats. (In fact, it has a little bit in common with the religious anti-humanist fervor, reflected in the actual Project 2025, that the best thing about us is what exists before we are even born and become human, but replacing innocence with infallibility.)

The second error, corollary to the first, is to deny the centrality of human effort and cognition to pure math. The entire point of the subject is the human understanding (and communication) of ideas and the “struggle and joy of discovering them ourselves” to quote Strogatz, though again I’d dispute the use of the word “discovering” here even if that is what it can feel like. (Heard at a conference — speaker: “I feel like Columbus”; audience member: “Wow, that’s modest.”) A better term would be “creating” (so: God rather than Columbus; also not modest).

Each philosopher in history has a unique feeling, a sort of idea cluster, associated with them, which was distilled from a lifetime spent struggling in this way, simplifying and consolidating a worldview according to their very human discernment, experience, vision and taste. This is not about the small collection of final results, but a manner of contemplation, evident throughout voluminous work, which brings transcendent perception in a way that is recognizable by other humans experiencing that work. Likewise, the exact final results are so unimportant for us in mathematics that we emulate the philosophical naming tradition, attaching to famous mathematicians a theorem or theory or object which captures their life’s interests even if it was not proved or defined in that form by them.

It certainly isn’t impossible to imagine a coalescence of our community around more human-centric norms: that pursuing one’s interests without AI remains in the interest of mathematical progress; and that its use for computations and literature searches that increase our cognitive load is also acceptable. But if our community pressures itself, in the name of scientific progress, to hand the slowest and most inconvenient part over to AI, I expect we lose the whole point of the endeavor. With the combined legacies of past struggles frozen in place, and mathematical grammar with them, the subject will begin to resemble Middle Earth at the end of the Third Age, with its inhabitants sailing through the Gates of Argonath and unable to comprehend their construction or the civilization that could build such things. Our monuments will stand, but as ghosts; and while their fellow citizens look for a time machine at the local Costco, someone still gets the computers to churn out papers on Hexagon4 with “no human understanding”.

I’ve restricted myself here to the question of using AI to do math, not to do things I personally think are legitimate — like running administrative reports, latexing handwritten notes, “vibe-coding” (ugh) tikz pictures, experimenting with examples — and things I do not think are acceptable — like writing a paper or a letter of recommendation, which represents our final attempt to communicate to other humans about an idea or about another human. If we don’t have the heart or the energy to do it ourselves, maybe on that point we should remain silent. Perhaps a necessary reaction to ChatGPT’s keyboard monkey explosion is that we (at least, we who have tenure) stop writing as if Stakhanovite productivity is the point and only write what is essential. This isn’t a promise that every paper I write from this point on will be important — there is plenty of “socially necessary” writing — but maybe the community as a whole can try to discuss what counts as beautiful exposition and recenter its writing around that.

In the background of Hokusai’s painting stands a snow-capped mountain, for this is only one of his famous 36 views of Mt. Fuji. Likewise, this will be one episode in the ongoing development of mathematics, which while difficult, will ultimately prove that what we do is not a game which can be solved. At its best, our subject is deeply social but not competitive, rigorous but not scientific, full of endless variety and individuation achieved through scaling the mind’s alpine wilderness. It is essential enough for society and for the human spirit that it will endure the present wave, and students who love it should not give up their dream of becoming a mathematician.

  1. The unofficial name given to OpenAI’s release of over 700 manuscripts on GitHub, none of them peer-reviewed, most of them not formalized, and several retracted since the release. ︎
  2. S. Strogatz, The Atlantic, October 25, https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/10/ai-math-human-future/689133/. I have long admired Strogatz for his outreach on behalf of the mathematics community. ︎
  3. Hardy, G. H. A Mathematician’s Apology. Cambridge University Press, 2012. First published 1940. ︎
  4. A new human-moderated platform for the online publication of preprints, modeled on the arXiv but designed to collect and organize work produced in concert with LLMs. https://hexagonmath.org ︎

Received 9 November 2026.

item.title: Letter to young mathematicians
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: What we are living through is a creative destruction, in which an old way of creating value is dismantled while a new one emerges. But this is also a major opportunity. Mathematicians are better positioned, and more needed, than at any point in history, I believe.
item.content:encoded:
Sinisa Slijepcevic, Professor at University of Zagreb and Founder & CEO, Cantab Pi.

AI disclosure

Statement of AI use: This letter has been written with the help of Claude. Sinisa provided the initial draft, and sharpened the argument and the citations in interaction with Claude Opus 5 High, used within Claude Projects. The entire chat is available at https://claude.ai/share/fc545e66-5222-4a82-b673-e2d8e3d7bbc4, and it’s inputs were this draft and this presentation in Croatian.

Dear young mathematician,

I want to share with you some thoughts on the future of mathematics.

I am writing because I sense that you are worried and afraid, and that you are asking what future there is for our field, and for you within it. Some of the most distinguished members of our community have given voice to exactly this mood in recent declarations and open letters.1 Their concerns are sincere, and many are real. But read together, these letters convey a sense of loss, and at times an instinct to turn the clock back. I see it differently. What we are living through is creative destruction, in which an old way of creating value is dismantled while a new one emerges.2 This is a major opportunity. Mathematicians are better positioned, and more needed, than at any point in history, I believe.

What we need to do comes down to three things. First, embrace AI, and shape its use in the interest of humanity and of the mathematical community, interests which I believe are fully aligned. Second, think bolder, asking questions that were out of reach until now and accepting what that implies. Third, put ourselves in the service of humanity, bringing our expertise in finding, describing and beautifying abstract structures to the many areas of mathematics, science, medicine and beyond where it is desperately needed.

1. Embrace AI

The order matters. First protect knowledge; then make mathematics efficient; then use AI as the foundation for effective collaboration, and with it for new models of credit, education, discovery and dissemination.

Protect knowledge. Use AI safely, as the leading enterprises already do, in controlled environments where your unpublished ideas are neither training data nor visible to others.3

Make mathematics efficient. Automate everything that can be automated. Mathematics is an extraordinarily inefficient enterprise, in how we retrieve information, do research, communicate and publish, and it has been ripe for transformation for a long time. Mathematicians spend a large share of their mental capacity on information that is now easily retrievable and on tasks that can now be automated.4 That capacity should be released and refocused on higher levels of cognition.

This will not leave mathematicians with nothing to do. AI can now settle hard, well-posed problems.5 But I agree with Peter Sarnak that AI is a long way from discovering genuinely new theories, that is, the abstractions, concepts and bodies of theorems through which we understand why things are true.6 That work needs human guidance. AI is a tool.

It follows that mathematics will have to change its system of values. Today the majority of the value we assign to a mathematical result is tied to its technical difficulty, and to that alone. This will now change. For example, if an off-the-shelf AI can prove a statement from a single prompt, that statement should perhaps be considered only a lemma. Other measures of a mathematical result’s “utility” will quickly emerge.7

Collaborate. AI makes possible effective systems of collaboration, and they are already emerging. Po-Ling Loh has proposed a publication model that rewards collective work by groups of experts rather than a race to publish.8 I would go further, towards partially closed, collaborative systems of AI-assisted research, with credit designed in from the start. Some fear this will make mathematics less open. It will not. Mathematicians have always built moats around their expertise, in how we write, in how our knowledge is organised and in our culture, and AI lowers them.9 The system of credit will have to adapt; that is a design problem, which will be solved hand in hand with the emergence of new notions of mathematical utility. The same holds for publishing, whose workflow has been outdated for decades and can now be re-engineered and prototyped quickly with the help of AI.10

2. Be bolder

We need to ask the questions we have been too scared to ask. Navier–Stokes is perhaps the best example.

On 8 September 2026, OpenAI released an AI-generated proof, formalised in Lean, that the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations with a smooth external force can develop a singularity in finite time: statements C and D of the Millennium Prize formulation.11 It is a remarkable achievement. But it establishes the existence of very special, isolated solutions, a set of measure zero in any reasonable sense, and tells us little about how fluids actually behave. Statements A and B, global regularity for the unforced equations, remain wide open and seem very far from solved. Because they are no longer needed to settle the prize, they are absent from the ongoing discussion of the result.

The question that truly matters, for mathematics and for the applied sciences, is a different one, namely to describe, in a suitable sense, the dynamics of the Navier–Stokes equation as a whole. I believe that understanding A and B will require exactly this. We are far from it even in two dimensions, without external force. As my friend Thierry Gallay has patiently explained to me, on the two-dimensional torus the flow relatively quickly organises itself into a finite set of Oseen vortices, and then into just two, which persist for a very long time.12 We can describe only special cases, for instance when the vortices are well separated.13 How vortices merge, and a full classification of the dynamics, are far out of reach. We lack even the language and the conjectures to formulate the question properly. In three dimensions it is almost certainly harder still.

More generally, our culture has rewarded incremental questions. Expert mathematicians have honed the crucial skill of choosing a problem that is solvable in reasonable time, yet worth pursuing for its mathematical utility. This skill now needs to be entirely reparametrised. Our goalposts must be far more ambitious, and we need to redefine what mathematical utility means.

Terence Tao has warned that AI is depleting our supply of good problems. In his view, problems are trivial to generate, but choosing those worth the effort depends on knowing a field’s difficulty landscape, and AI is flattening it.14 I disagree with the conclusion. AI will hoover up many of the problems we have been asking so far; by construction, most of them were incremental or not ambitious enough. But AI can also help us generate many, many new problems, and then, and this is the essential step, help us prioritise them by a new notion of utility, for mathematics and for humanity. The landscape is not disappearing. It is being redrawn, and it is ours to map.

3. Serve humanity

The key skill of mathematicians is more needed than ever, namely to find abstract structure in chaos, to describe it, and then to beautify it, that is, to make it sharp and precise, and therefore useful and ripe for the next level of abstraction. The complexity around us keeps growing, and so does the need.

Let me give an example. AlphaFold, for which Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is universally presented as a triumph of AI. I read it differently, as a triumph of mathematics. Open the paper and the code and see what the algorithm is actually made of.

A protein is first encoded as tensors, namely a representation of its multiple sequence alignment, and a pairwise representation of every pair of residues. Building the alignment is a combinatorial search through genetic and structural databases for evolutionary relatives of the given sequence. The statistical signal extracted from it is coevolution, the tendency of positions that mutate together to sit close together in space.

The pair representation is then treated as a graph whose edges are updated in triangles, so that the inferred relations between residues i, j, k remain geometrically consistent, as the triangle inequality demands. Geometry enters through an orthonormal frame attached to each residue, built by Gram–Schmidt, with an attention mechanism designed to be invariant under the rigid motions of space, SE(3). The rotations of these frames are updated as quaternions.15

Probability is the language of the output. The first AlphaFold predicted, for every pair of residues, a full probability distribution over their distance (the “distogram”), turned these distributions into a potential, and found the structure by gradient descent.16 The final step of AlphaFold 2 is classical physics, namely a gradient flow minimising the energy of the Amber force field.17

The core structures rely on graph theory, differential geometry, algebra, probability, statistics and the calculus of variations. The learning machinery that fits them to roughly 100,000 experimentally determined protein structures is, in my view, the least novel ingredient of the construction. The breakthrough lay in finding, describing and beautifying the right structures. The same toolkit runs through the neighbouring work on protein design.18

Here is a challenge for you. Build an algorithm that matches AlphaFold’s accuracy using these mathematical structures together with classical, transparent statistical and optimisation tools, with no black box. I am convinced this is feasible. It may open the door to far more ambitious questions about protein interactions and reactions. It would also help explain why so many attempts to carry AlphaFold’s success over to other problems in chemistry and biology have disappointed. They copied the black box and neglected the step that mattered, namely recognising and describing the structure inherent in the problem.19

The same programme applies far more widely.

First, mathematical knowledge itself. We need better structures for it, optimised for retrieval and discovery. That is certainly not arXiv. Nor is it Lean, since the power of mathematics lies in hierarchical abstraction, not only in encoding truth. Lean is an excellent truth-checker, but nothing more.20

Furthermore, modern theoretical physics rests on mathematical foundations that are still not consistent. The infinities of quantum field theory are cancelled by renormalisation, which has never been made rigorous in the generality physics needs.21 Nathan Seiberg, one of the architects of modern quantum field theory, stressed again this spring that, despite its enormous success, the theory still lacks a satisfactory, mathematically rigorous formulation.22 Where mathematicians have found the right structures, rigour has followed, and new mathematics with it.23 I believe that resolving these inconsistencies would open doors to a better understanding of physical reality.

Consider biology, chemistry and medicine. Clinical trials still rest largely on two-sample tests whose foundations are more than a century old,24 and most clinical guidelines are decision trees three or four levels deep. Even regulators now recognise that modern statistical methods, Bayesian methods among them, must become part of how trials are designed and judged.25 And no, AI will not solve this on its own. AI-discovered molecules now pass early safety trials at high rates, but efficacy trials, which depend on understanding the biology, far less so; and the leading structure-prediction models still reproduce their training data rather than the physics.26 We hold vast amounts of data about human biology and health, but by modern standards it is of extremely low quality and poorly structured.27 Before AI can help, someone must first find, describe and beautify the structures within it. That will be a mathematician.

Your time

So, my friend, young mathematician: do not despair. Learn. Use AI. Be brave. Reach lands that none of us has yet been able to imagine.

This is your time.

Received 7 October 202628.

  1. The Leiden Declaration (2 June 2026), leidendeclaration.ai; “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics” (11 September 2026), a declaration whose 25 initial signatories are all Fields Medallists, see terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/11; the open letter of 42 mathematician Fellows of the Royal Society to the President of the Royal Society, Sir Paul Nurse (September 2026); K. Ono, address to the National Academy of Sciences (2026), as reported by P.-L. Loh (note 8), predicting that within three to five years theoretical mathematical research will shrink to a small fraction, with the remaining academics working more like humanities scholars. ︎
  2. J. A. Schumpeter, Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), ch. 7, “The Process of Creative Destruction”; C. M. Christensen, The Innovator’s Dilemma (Harvard Business School Press, 1997). Christensen’s mechanism fits mathematics closely, since incumbents fail because they keep optimising what their established audience values (for us, technical difficulty) while a new entrant redefines what is valuable. ︎
  3. Leading enterprises deploy AI in controlled environments in which prompts and data are isolated and not used to train models, for example through managed cloud services such as Amazon Bedrock. The need is not hypothetical. In September 2026 the race to the Navier–Stokes result was triggered by a rumour about unpublished work, and OpenAI subsequently published an investigation into whether user inputs could have influenced its result (note 11). Tao has warned that even the rumour of someone working on a problem can now trigger a massive AI-powered effort to “flatten” it (note 14). ︎
  4. Anyone who has spent days or weeks verifying the precise statement of a needed technical lemma, reconstructing the exact meaning of every object through several layers of hard-to-retrieve published work, knows how much of our mental load goes on retrieval and bookkeeping. This is precisely the work that can now be automated. ︎
  5. In May 2026 an OpenAI model disproved the Erdős unit-distance conjecture, a question some eighty years old; the disproof was verified by outside mathematicians including Tim Gowers (OpenAI, “Model disproves discrete geometry conjecture”, May 2026), and within the same week Anthropic’s Claude Mythos produced an independent proof (Decrypt, 9 September 2026). On 1–2 August 2026 OpenAI released results by its unreleased Astra model on ten problems open for at least a decade, including three Erdős problems, each with a Lean 4 proof and a 249-page manuscript; peer review is pending, and mathematicians have noted that some results lean heavily on earlier work. On 10 August 2026 Anthropic reported that an unreleased Claude research model raised the proven lower bound for the proportion of zeros of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%, with a Lean formalisation, examined by Brian Conrey and Dan Goldston (anthropic.com/research/riemann-zeta). On 7 September 2026 L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster, working with Claude and other models, released a blow-up result for the forced Euler equations, and the next day OpenAI released its Navier–Stokes result (note 11). ︎
  6. P. Sarnak, “Peter Sarnak on ‘The AlphaZero Test’ for Mathematics”, Notices of the AMS 73(7) (2026), doi:10.1090/noti3373. In the test, one gives a theorem prover with no access to outside data or theory an elementary statement, such as the Ramanujan conjecture in Ramanujan’s own formulation, and asks whether it is true. Sarnak predicts failure for most theorems whose proofs rely on abstraction and on the bodies of theorems we call theories; in his view AI will do mathematics as Stockfish plays chess, not as AlphaZero does. ︎
  7. On the shift in values see H. Cohn, “The technical debt of AI-generated mathematics”, and G. Sanderson, “If math is more than proof, we need to better celebrate the rest of it”, guest posts on terrytao.wordpress.com (15 and 18 September 2026). Tao has proposed labelling certain problems “analysis-required”, so that a bare answer without illuminating reasoning counts for little (note 14). I welcome these proposals; my point is that new measures of utility should be designed deliberately, not only defensively. ︎
  8. P.-L. Loh, “AI, From Competition to Collaboration”, IMS Bulletin, 1 September 2026. Loh proposes journals that accept only papers produced jointly by a sufficient group of experts in a sub-area, lightly reviewed for significance by researchers from another area. The precedent is the Polymath project: T. Gowers and M. Nielsen, “Massively collaborative mathematics”, Nature 461, 879–881 (2009). ︎
  9. The moats are cultural. We write up novel research with a premium on elegance, which partially hides or camouflages the reasoning that led to it. Our knowledge is organised in ways that are hard to navigate (note 4). We also celebrate solitary secrecy; Andrew Wiles worked on Fermat’s Last Theorem in near-total secrecy for about seven years (S. Singh, Fermat’s Last Theorem, 1997). One can argue that AI is making mathematics more open and accessible, not less. ︎
  10. The IT systems used by most mathematics publishers are obsolete, and the workflow of submission, refereeing, revision and typesetting has barely changed in decades. New workflows and systems can be prototyped relatively quickly with the help of AI. ︎
  11. OpenAI, “On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem”, 8 September 2026, with a paper and a Lean formalisation. OpenAI states that the result establishes statement C (and D) of the official problem description (C. Fefferman, claymath.org); it does not intend to claim the prize, and the Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list the problem as active. Statements C and D allow a smooth external force; A and B (global regularity on ℝ³ and on the torus) concern the unforced equations and remain open. See also L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster (7 September 2026) on blow-up for the forced Euler equations, and OpenAI’s companion result on the unforced Euler equations. ︎
  12. T. Gallay, personal communication. The numerical picture goes back to W. H. Matthaeus et al., “Selective decay and coherent vortices in two-dimensional incompressible turbulence”, Phys. Rev. Lett. 66, 2731 (1991). On the Oseen vortex as the universal long-time attractor in the plane, see T. Gallay and C. E. Wayne, “Global stability of vortex solutions of the two-dimensional Navier–Stokes equation”, Comm. Math. Phys. 255, 97–129 (2005). ︎
  13. T. Gallay, “Interaction of vortices in weakly viscous planar flows”, Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 200, 445–490 (2011). ︎
  14. T. Tao, Mathstodon post, 8 September 2026, reported by Decrypt, 9 September 2026. Tao answers the objection that infinitely many problems exist with the analogy that a region can suffer a shortage of drinking water while surrounded by ocean. See also his curated summary of views at teorth.github.io/tao-web/ai-views.html (updated 17 September 2026). The prioritisation step I propose is aimed at exactly this point. ︎
  15. J. Jumper et al., “Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold”, Nature 596, 583–589 (2021), and its Supplementary Information (Algorithms 21–23: rigid frames by Gram–Schmidt, invariant point attention, quaternion backbone updates); code at github.com/deepmind/alphafold. Hassabis and Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with David Baker. ︎
  16. A. W. Senior et al., “Improved protein structure prediction using potentials from deep learning”, Nature 577, 706–710 (2020). ︎
  17. AlphaFold repository, Amber relaxation step: energy minimisation with OpenMM. ︎
  18. J. Ingraham, V. Garg, R. Barzilay and T. Jaakkola, “Generative Models for Graph-Based Protein Design”, NeurIPS 2019. Local frames, quaternions, autoregressive probability and likelihood-based statistics all appear there. ︎
  19. A black box that reproduces its training data, without capturing the structure of the underlying problem, works where a new case resembles what it has seen and fails where it does not. The first two examples apply AlphaFold to neighbouring questions; the last two concern its extension to protein–ligand complexes.
    (i) Mutations. A single amino-acid change barely alters the sequence but can unfold a protein. A model that had captured the physics of folding would register this; a model that matches sequences to known structures returns the familiar fold. The AlphaFold database itself states that AlphaFold has not been validated for predicting the effects of mutations, and for five patient variants of antithrombin with documented folding defects it returned the native structure every time (“Analysis of AlphaFold and molecular dynamics structure predictions of mutations in serpins”, PLOS ONE, 2024).
    (ii) Proteins with two folds. Some proteins switch between two distinct structures. D. Chakravarty et al., “AlphaFold predictions of fold-switched conformations are driven by structure memorization”, Nat. Commun. 15, 7296 (2024), show that AlphaFold finds the second fold when it is present in its training data, not by inferring it; it recalls rather than explains.
    (iii) Ligands. M. R. Masters, A. H. Mahmoud and M. A. Lill, “Investigating whether deep learning models for co-folding learn the physics of protein–ligand interactions”, Nat. Commun. 16, 8854 (2025), mutated or removed the residues that hold a ligand in place, so that physically it could no longer bind. AlphaFold 3 and similar models often still placed the ligand in its original pose, reproducing a remembered complex rather than the interaction.
    (iv) Prospective drug screening. In “Large scale prospective evaluation of co-folding across 557 Mac1–ligand complexes and three virtual screens”, eLife reviewed preprint (March 2026), co-folding succeeded roughly in proportion to how similar a target was to its training structures, while classical docking, which models the physical interaction explicitly, performed surprisingly well. In every case the model is reliable only within the range of what it has already seen. ︎
  20. Tao has observed that once a well-curated database of precise problems exists, others can build on it systematically, by human and AI means alike (terrytao.wordpress.com, 22 January 2026, on the Erdős problems database), a small precedent for what better structures for mathematical knowledge could achieve. Formal verification is becoming routine; in September 2026 a formalisation of the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem was reported (Decrypt, 9 September 2026). This is why structure and abstraction, not truth-checking, is the scarce resource. ︎
